en: The Sūtra on the Self-Exposition of the Past Deeds of the Five Hundred Disciples of the Buddha, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Regarding the Dragon King Anavatapta, his name in the Jin language is Wufen (Unburning); during the time when the Buddha was in the world, he received a prediction as a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, he possesses the virtue of divine ferocity and dwells upon the ruins of Mount Kunlun.

This is the palace and jeweled hall where the Dragon resides; he oversees the sources of the five rivers, where there is a pond of eight-flavored water with flowers of seven colors. Those who drink this water immediately gain knowledge of their past lives.

At that time, the Dragon King invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One, along with his five hundred foremost disciples. After the meal was finished, they sat upon lotus flowers, and [the Buddha] recounted the origins of the transgressions and merits they had created in past lives: how even the most minute deeds result in karmic retributions that persist through kalpas and eons, making it impossible to save oneself, such that only by encountering a Perfectly Enlightened One can one attain deliverance from the world.
Each composed a verse and uttered this praise:
"The Buddha, supreme among men, is the Charioteer of the Dharma; Having severed the prison of the fetters, he wanders in Śrāvastī.
His faculties are tranquil and his virtue is majestic; The Tathāgata himself addresses his bhikṣus:"
"There are various spirits who find delight therein, with countless varieties of diverse flowers;
the four great rivers surge forth toward the four quarters, and all those flowing streams return to the oceans and seas."
I am Hatthigāma-Isidatta; though men cannot reach this place, I have arrived by means of my supernormal power.
My flight is swift, for I have already crossed over; come quickly together to that deep-flowing pool.
The bhikṣu said:
“Excellent; I shall obey your command.
Having heard your venerable instruction, I shall mount my supernormal power (ṛddhi), just as a king of geese leads a flock of geese.”
He travels and wanders through rivers and streams, joyfully observing the various beings as they enjoy themselves;
the Buddha, the God among Gods, is likewise, soaring through the air together with his disciples.
The Buddha went to his disciples and told them:
"Do you recognize those who have passed through previous lives? Tell me each of whom has practiced such conduct that they have obtained immeasurable merit."
That Kāśyapa, a benevolent disciple of the Buddha, is like a lion traversing deep mountains;
wherever he goes, none dare oppose him, as he then speaks of the deeds performed in his previous lives.

"I gathered wild oats from the field; having given a small portion to a Pratyekabuddha, my mind attained the joy of liberation, free from outflows, as I honored the practice of emptiness with a tranquil mind."
At that time, he formed this aspiration in his mind; immediately thereafter, he contemplated the supreme Dharma.
Having associated with such a person, at the end of this life, he was reborn in Uttarakuru.
By virtue of the merit resulting from those causes and conditions, he passed through a thousand more rebirths in Uttarakuru,
and was subsequently born in the Heaven of Exalted Life (*Śubhakṛtsna*), where he was preeminent and without equal.
By means of the merit created through those blessings, I was likewise reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven a thousand times;
adorned with various flowers, perfumes, and precious necklaces, my body was subtle, beautiful, and sovereign.
Having ended their lives in the heavens, they were then reborn in Uttarakuru;
this was due to the power of their former vows and because of these roots of merit they had cultivated.
Born into a wealthy family of the Brahmin caste, with immeasurable wealth and vast undertakings, he felt no craving amidst the five pleasures; toward this Buddha, he was peerless.
The Dharma taught by the Great Compassionate One— The various powers, single-minded concentration, and the faculties;
The seven factors of enlightenment and the practice of the eightfold path— It is for the purpose of attaining this Dharma.
Having exhausted all outflows, holding lamps in hand, they shall be among the very last of this assembly;
meeting together with upright conduct and free from evil, the Buddha—the Tathāgata—has spoken what is good.
Those who uphold the prohibitions and precepts attain their aspirations;
whatever they seek according to their intentions, my final body shall be fully perfected, so that birth and death may be exhausted and their very roots uprooted.
I have severed all fetters of craving; thus I am a prince of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Foremost in contentment, I constantly contemplate the Way; my mind is empty, pure, and free from attachment.
My resolve is firm and unshakable, like a great mountain that cannot be moved.
Thus the Venerable Kāśyapa, amidst the assembly of bhikṣus at the great lake Anavatapta,
spoke of his own past karmic conditions:
"When I lived as a rishi in seclusion, I saw a śramaṇa there."
Seeing the Pratyekabuddha, most venerable one,
clad in robes of crimson, my heart was filled with joy;
I washed his garments for him and further sewed his *kāṣāya*, repeatedly prostrating before him.
He then took pity on me and flew into the midst of the sky;
emitting water and fire from above and below, he suddenly vanished in an instant.
I immediately joined my palms and made this vow within my own heart:
"May I attain such as this: clarity and great wisdom.
May I not be born into a noble family, nor may I be born into a lowly lineage;
may I always be born into a middle-class family, with the aspiration to become a śramaṇa."
By virtue of these merits, for five hundred lifetimes I have always attained a human body and, in every birth, become a śramaṇa.
In this final lifetime, I have once again returned to the human race.
Having encountered and beheld the Perfectly Awakened One, the unsurpassed Teacher,
he then became a śramaṇa; in the presence of the Lion of the Śākyas,
he attained arhatship and entered the cool state of parinirvāṇa.
Now, before the eyes of the World-Honored One, amidst the assembly of bhikṣus,
you discourse upon the excellence of my wisdom and turn the wheel of the True Dharma.
As for Śāriputra’s wisdom, before the assembly of bhikṣus—
At the great lake Anavatapta, he himself recounted his past conduct:
"When I was a rishi dwelling in seclusion, residing among the forest trees,
a man came there and requested that I become a śramaṇa for him."
I shaved off his hair and beard, washed his robes, sewed them, and dyed them; my heart was filled with joy within.
He withdrew to one side and sat down cross-legged.
I then attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha and immediately flew into the void.
At that time, I made this vow:
"May my body attain supernormal powers; may I obtain such great strength and great supernormal powers as these."
By virtue of this merit, in every place of rebirth,
whether among gods or humans, they shall illuminate the deeds they have performed.
Then, in their final existence, having attained a human body, they shall reach [enlightenment].
Having encountered the Perfectly Awakened One, the unsurpassed Teacher,
he became a śramaṇa under the Lion of the Śākyas;
thus he attained arhatship, reaching the cool state of parinirvāṇa.
Having performed very little good, yet obtaining immeasurable peace and security;
yet I have also committed unwholesome deeds—listen now as I speak of them.
Departing from Rājagṛha to the east, I was born as the son of a nobleman.
Going outside the house to play, I went from house to house seeking food and drink.
There I saw my parents, the two of them enjoying each other’s company;
as soon as they saw me, they beat me and, reviling me, drove me away.
Merely by means of right livelihood, yet failing to put it into practice in one's own body,
one falls into the Black Rope Hell and undergoes incalculable suffering.
Due to the remaining karmic retribution of that, in this final life,
The various heterodox paths of other schools beat their bodies until they are crushed like reeds;
I shall, through this illness, bring my life to its end and attain parinirvāṇa,
so that the remaining karmic retributions they have created may finally be extinguished.
Therefore, one should gladden the heart and serve one's parents with supreme filial piety;
because of this joyful heart, a person attains a realm superior to the heavens.
Thus, the Venerable Kolita, among the assembly of bhikṣus—
At the great lake Anavatapta, he himself recounted his past causes and conditions:
"In the past, when I went to a monastery, I saw a place where the ground was impure.
I immediately took up my broom and swept that temple building."
Having finally beheld the purity of the monastery, my heart was filled with great joy;
it has rendered me free from defilement, just as this temple is pure.
By virtue of this merit, in whatever place I am born, may I remain thus undefiled.
My facial complexion was harmonious and lovely, Elegant and beyond compare.
As for my other blessings, In this final life,
my parents named me And gave me the title "Pure Elimination."
Among my kinsmen, I was pure at birth;
loved and revered by all, those who saw me never grew weary.
It is worthy to behold the Perfectly Awakened One, the unsurpassed Teacher.
Having already become an Arhat, cool and attained parinirvāṇa;
this is my aspiration—that I may be free from defilement.
Now, as an Arhat free from stain, I have accomplished what was to be done and am without outflows.
Even if one were to sweep this entire world until it is pure,
it would not equal the merit of sweeping the path where one who has abandoned desire walks.
Even if one were to sweep the whole world, it would not equal the merit of sweeping the place where a practitioner of the Way walks.
It is not equal to sweeping a single step of ground for the Sangha of the four quarters.
Even if one were to sweep all the monasteries throughout the world,
it would not equal sweeping a single step of ground at a Buddhist temple.
The merit I have created through my body is known by this distinction;
as I sweep the Buddhist temple, my heart is filled with joy.
By understanding this, one realizes that the Way and virtue of the Perfectly Awakened One are sublime.
When one serves a Buddhist temple, the merit obtained is exceedingly great.

It is only when you, my friend, keep this in mind that you will realize how the wholesome deeds performed in the past have brought about these actual fruits: a state of satisfaction, peace, and happiness.
Therefore, for the sake of the Buddhist temple, those who serve it with a pure heart—O Benevolent One, this is foremost; there is no field of merit superior to this.
By being able to serve it in this way, one attains immeasurable peace.
All have been destroyed and eliminated: all lust, anger, and delusion.
With a mind of non-contempt and joy, how could one’s merit be slight?
This is directed toward the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, and all the disciples of the Buddhas.
Thus Cūḍapanthaka, standing before the bhikṣus at the great lake Anavatapta,
spoke of his own past causes: "Formerly,
when I went out for a stroll, I was accompanied by my kinsmen and friends."
Wearing ornaments upon his head and *sumanā* flowers on his ears,
the Buddha Viśvabhū established a great monastery there;
from afar he beheld the multitude of people dwelling together and serving him.
My kinsmen and friends set out from home together, each carrying fine flowers;
with pure hearts, they all scattered them as offerings at that Buddhist temple.
Seeing such extensive giving, I too then first resolved my mind [upon awakening].
He then took flowers from the forest and offered them to the Buddhist temple.
Wherever he was reborn, he did not fall into lower realms; ascending to heaven, he became a human being.
Because of this root of merit, all that he does is clearly illuminated.
Later, he encountered the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the unsurpassed Teacher;
having realized the fruit of Arhatship, he attained the coolness of Nirvāṇa.
Having offered but a single flower, he further gained [the merit of] a hundred thousand years.
One enjoys oneself in the heavens through one's own merit, and through remaining blessings attains Nirvāṇa.
Had I known from the outset that the Buddha’s merit is immeasurable, I would have immediately erected stūpas and monasteries; such merit would have been without limit.
Not necessarily with a joyful heart, their merit remains but slight.
Only when I mindfully recollect this— the merit performed by my own body— before the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and all the disciples of the Buddhas, [is it truly great].
Now that I have attained the true fruition, my mind is contented, joyful, and at peace.
Because of these practiced deeds, birth shall finally cease and never arise again;
free from outflows and without attachment, I have attained the coolness of Nirvana.
The five realms of existence are exhausted; no longer shall one enter a womb again.
This is the final birth; thus, there shall be no further arising.
Having liberated oneself from the root of birth and death, one has already crossed over all the oceans of existence.
Now, by reason of this, I have obtained the name Sumana.
At that time, the elder Sumana was present among the assembly of monks at Lake Anavatapta,
where he himself recounted his past deeds.
"In the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, in the land of Bandhumatī,
[he] originally established a single chamber for the Saṃgha from the four directions.
Furthermore, he provided bedding and furnishings, all of which he offered as a gift."
Having rejoiced in his heart, he immediately made this vow:
"May I see the Samyaksaṃbuddha and be permitted to become a śramaṇa;
may I attain the unsurpassed unconditioned state, the cool and perfect nirvāṇa."
This is the root of meritorious virtue; for ninety-one kalpas he dwelt in peace.
Having attained spontaneous vision, he abides in the heavens and the world.
As for his remaining merits and blessings, in this final life, they have now come to fruition.
Born into the family of a wealthy elder, Proud and noble, with no brothers;
Born to be revered by his father, He immediately heard the father’s instruction:
"I bestow my son as a gift, Along with billions of kinds of precious treasuries."
Extraordinary hair grows on the soles of his feet, naturally reaching four inches in length;
his body is supple and beautiful, stable and secure, free from harm.
For ninety past kalpas, and for as many more to come, it shall remain thus.
My body was unaware, as I raised my foot to step upon the earth.
Now, in this final birth, I have again attained a human form;
having achieved non-attachment, I am cooled and enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha, seeing me everywhere, declared: "In diligence you are foremost and supreme;
liberated and with all outflows exhausted, you have already attained the immovable state.
Thus, O Koliyan, you stand in the midst of the Saṃgha.
At Lake Anavatapta, he himself recounted his original merits:
"I did not understand merit, nor did I originally know its meaning;
yet, seeing the temple of the Buddha Vipaśyin, I made offerings and served him."
Golden temples with the hue of purple-gold, and banners, parasols, incense, and flowers—
by seeing and making offerings to these stupas and monasteries, one attains birth in a good realm.
Constantly dwelling among gods and humans, whatever one does shall be clearly perceived.
Throughout ninety-one kalpas, he never returned to the evil realms.
Having performed even a small amount of meritorious deeds, he obtained vast and manifold peace.
Having attained non-attachment, his parinirvāṇa was pure and cool.
Had I known from the beginning that the Buddha’s merit was such as this,
I would have constantly made offerings to the stupas and monasteries, and the merit obtained would have surpassed this.
Therefore, by means of clear knowledge, one realizes that the virtue of the Perfectly Awakened One is vast and sublime.
When one makes offerings to stupas and monasteries, their merit is without end.
The Buddha, seeing all, has declared me to be foremost among those who delight in the sutras;
possessing manifold learning, my eloquence and virtue reach the ultimate truth.
At that time, the Elder Vṛddha, who had previously been among the assembly of monks at Lake Anavatapta, spoke of his own past deeds:
"In my former life, through my parents, I was born as the most honored among sons."
I respectfully serve my father, and likewise provide filial care for my mother.
To both parents, as well as sisters and younger brothers, slaves, guests, and servants—I speak thus on behalf of my parents:
provide them with food and drink at the proper times.
At that time, giving rise to thoughts of greed and envy, one should not eat the flesh of one’s parents;
yet through words of anger and slander, one may obtain food and wealth.
Due to the sins committed on this account, one falls into the Great Mountain Hell.
Roasted and scorched within the Black Rope Hell, their further sufferings are beyond reckoning.
Emerging from that hell, in every place where they are reborn throughout successive lifetimes,
they constantly suffer from great hunger and thirst, perishing of starvation amidst diligent toil.
In this final birth, having returned to obtain a human body,
I have encountered the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the unsurpassed Teacher.
Under the Lion of the Śākyas, I have already become a śramaṇa.
Having attained the path of non-attachment, you shall reach the cool state of parinirvāṇa.
O Benevolent One, it is only here that I, with my supernormal power of flight, shall return to this cave; only then will I obtain food.
Therefore, one should rejoice and serve one's parents;
with a single mind, prostrate in worship, and one’s blessings will be immeasurable.
O Benevolent One, remember me, and cut away my evil deeds.
All receive the fruits they have sown; neither sin nor merit can be escaped.
Piṇḍola closed his door, yet now he is present among the assembly at Lake Anavatapta, where he speaks of his own past deeds.
"In a former life, I was the son of a noble householder in the kingdom of Pāṇḍubhūmi;
my clan possessed abundant wealth and treasures, and I was surrounded by a vast retinue.
Standing in the presence of the king, I enjoyed unsurpassed happiness."
One of upright countenance brings joy to those who see him; his complexion is beyond compare.
At that time, I set out with my carriage, preceded and followed by a multitude of attendants, wishing to travel about for sightseeing, accompanied by a host of court ladies.
While wandering and observing there, I saw a śramaṇa whose appearance was serene;
he practiced the deportment of tranquility and wore saffron-colored robes.
When I saw that śramaṇa, I gave rise to an evil thought.
One loathes their physical form, filled with anger and lacking joy.
Why have you shaved off your beard and hair? Your countenance is dark and ugly;
your body is plagued by boils and scabs; why are both body and mind so weak and exhausted?
Because of the sins committed through such speech and the utterance of evil words,
after his life there has ended, he shall fall into hell.
Even when he escapes from that hell, his complexion will be dark and hideous.
With boils, abscesses, and scabies upon their bodies, both body and mind are emaciated and exhausted.
Grasping earthen vessels, they beg for alms;
they wear discarded clothes from the dead, garments that are tattered, coarse, and filthy, having no place of rest.
Wherever he wished to go, seeking only to beg for his daily sustenance,
he was met with the brandishing of staves and harsh rebukes;
thus he was treated with jealousy and contempt by others throughout five hundred lifetimes, in every place where he was born.
Constantly impoverished and famished, he died of hunger through his toil and suffering.
Then he beheld the Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus,
together with the great assembly, preaching the words of the nectar of immortality.
Just as he saw the great assembly, he quickly ran toward it,
desiring therein to obtain food and drink. Upon reaching the place where the great assembly was gathered,
he saw that they were all seated, wishing to hear the Dharma.
Failing to obtain even a portion of his original vow, and having received no offerings of food, the Tathāgata, moved by great compassion, spoke to him, saying:
"Virtuous one, welcome here; come, sit upon this seat."
I was then filled with joy and leaped for gladness; with single-minded devotion, I joined my palms and bowed my head at the feet of the World-Honored One, then withdrew to sit to one side.
Thereupon, the Honored One, in his great compassion, Gautama of supreme kindness and pity, [spoke].
He explained them in successive order, preaching the Four Truths for my sake.
The Able One (Śākyamuni) shaved off my hair and beard; through this, I perceived the path.
The Buddha ordained me as a śramaṇa, and thereupon I attained supernormal powers.
For this reason, my title and name are called Cājja;
because of this, the Buddha declared me to be foremost in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
The Buddha is the valiant Great Honored One, the World Hero, the most supreme.
With infinite compassion through his supernormal powers, he delivers us from manifold sufferings.
"Welcome, O Honored One," they said; thus, while among the assembly of monks at Lake Anavatapta, he himself recounted his past deeds.
"To the east of the city of Rājagṛha, there once lived a wealthy man.
At a time when grain was scarce and prices were high, a wandering ascetic came to that place.
While I was sitting alone eating, a noble ascetic arrived."
Having shattered the conditions for solitary awakening, he has attained mastery and the state beyond outflows.
Yet, giving rise to thoughts of greed and envy, his mind is intent on evil.
Now that this bhikṣu has arrived, how could he possibly be in accord with the Year-Spirit?
Thereupon, thinking of food and drink, he mixed it with horse dung;
after the practitioner had eaten it, his life ended immediately.
When my own life came to an end, I fell into hell for a very long time.
In the Saṃghāta and Raurava hells, they are roasted and boiled life after life.
Having escaped from these hells, they once again obtain a human body;
yet their bodies are constantly plagued by many diseases, and they pass away in a state of anguish.
Thus, for five hundred lifetimes, in every place where he was born,
he suffered from illness and constant misfortune, passing away in anguish.
Finally, in this last life, he has been born among human beings.
He again beheld the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the unsurpassed Teacher.
He left the household life to become a śramaṇa and received the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having already attained the path of Arhatship, he entered the coolness of parinirvāṇa.
Regarding this benevolent one, his supernormal powers are free from outflows;
yet his body is plagued by many ailments, and wherever he stays, there is no peace.
Thereupon, he fully recollects and reflects upon all the deeds he performed in the past.
All have obtained their respective fruits; neither sin nor merit can be escaped.
Thus the venerable Nanda, amidst the assembly of bhikṣus, by the Lake Anavatapta, spoke of his own past deeds.
Long ago, there was a practitioner who entered a village to beg for alms.
Seeing a dead woman, her body was bluish, bloated, and exceedingly foul-smelling.
He sat cross-legged and contemplated the transformations of impermanence.
Reflecting on the impurity of decay, he focused his will to train the mind in concentration.
Then, while sitting there, a subtle sound arose;
hearing this noise, he became terrified, and from that state of single-mindedness, he emerged.
Seeing the dead with the belly decomposed and ruined, Foul secretions and impurities flowing from the various orifices, the stench unbearable to endure.
The intestines, stomach, and five viscera are exposed; The heart and liver are all scattered and severed.
Having observed the countless, innumerable worms, one returns to stillness of mind.
Examining the dead body outside, one reflects inwardly upon one’s own frame:
"That is so, and I am thus; when reckoned to their source, all are empty and non-existent."
Since arising from samādhi, I have practiced without indolence;
I have neither gone out for alms nor thought of food and drink.
Even if I were to enter a village to seek sustenance, [I would do so with such mindfulness].
Though one may see a beautiful form, one should contemplate it as foul and impure.
Beholding all such shapes and colors, they are no different from a dead person;
examining their nature of decay and ruin, there is nothing in them to be delighted in.
I thought and acted thus, thereby attaining freedom from craving and desire;
I followed and observed the four brahma-vihāras, reflecting deeply and never engaging in frivolity.
When my life there came to an end, I immediately ascended to the Brahma Heaven.
When his lifespan in the Brahma realm had ended, he descended to be born in Vārāṇasī.
He became the son of a powerful and noble elder;
born into that family, he was respected by all, [practicing] the perfection of right reception.
One should practice diligently by day and remain sleepless at night;
when seeing many women, one should view them all equally as a heap of rotting matter.
Those who lie down to sleep with drums for pillows, and those musicians holding lutes—[all such things are but vanity].
Musical instruments are scattered upon the ground; dreams and fantasies are but idle chatter.
Therein one reflects upon past thoughts and the virtuous deeds performed in former lives, contemplating the impurity of the realms of perception and the experiences traversed in previous existences.
Having observed this, my mind sought the state of desirelessness;
pressed by these circumstances, O virtuous one, I have departed from you.
Immediately rising from my bed, I descended from the palace and fled to avoid him.
The devas took pity on me, and their gate opened spontaneously.
At that time, I departed from the city and went to the banks of the flowing water;
looking afar toward the opposite shore, I saw the śramaṇa Śāntamūla.
Furthermore, seeing the Great Śramaṇa, he raised his voice and cried out, informing him of his own misery and distress:
"I have abandoned desire through my supernormal powers.
With a voice that was profound and gentle, the World-Honored One spoke these words in response to his words of suffering:
"Come, child, do not fear; here there is no end to suffering.
Abandon all mental afflictions and cross over to the other shore.
Go to where the Great Compassionate One dwells, the World-Honored One, the peerless person."
Exquisite and peerless, like one who is hungry and thirsty,
he immediately understood its meaning upon hearing it.
Having seen the Truth of the Path therein, he sought from the Buddha to leave the household life.
Gautama, out of great compassion, Permitted me to become a śramaṇa.
In the course of a single night, as the dawn was breaking,
All taints were exhausted, and I attained the coolness of parinirvāṇa.
This is the wholesome conduct I performed in my previous lives;
this is my final birth, and I have attained the track of the Deathless.
Thus spoke the noble son Yaśas, possessed of supernormal powers.
At Lake Anavatapta, he himself recounted his past deeds:
"In the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, after Kāśyapa Buddha had entered nirvāṇa,
King Jitāri erected a stūpa, constructed of the seven treasures and exceedingly vast."
At that time, among the sons of the king, there was a crown prince;
at that time, I was the Honored Buddha, the first to erect the pillar of the stūpa.
By virtue of this merit, in every place where I was born throughout successive lifetimes,
Whether in heaven or among humans, their merit will naturally manifest.
In every place where they are born, they will find their lands exceedingly prosperous;
with wealth beyond measure, they will always delight in great generosity.
Throughout five hundred lifetimes, I practiced giving without any sense of stinginess,
providing for the common people, the śramaṇas, and the brahmins. Following the path of the pratyekabuddhas,
I became free from craving and desire, reaching the state of outflowlessness (anāsrava).
With a pure and joyful heart, he made offerings to an assembly of five hundred.
By virtue of this merit, in this final birth, he was born into the noble Śākya clan; at the appropriate time, he spoke these words:
"Whatever treasures there may be in my home, Money, wealth, and material goods—
I shall give them all away To fully relieve the poor.
I shall provide for those who are weary and insatiable, And bring succor to all who are lowly."
Fu Shanjian replied in answer: "How could I have anything to bestow?
When my words were heard within the house, they were filled with grief and terror;
they fled in all directions to the eight quarters, and the wet nurses all departed."
Out of affection and love, my mother immediately said to me:
"For the sake of devas, humans, ghosts, and spirits, why do you say you are so gravely ill?
At that time, I replied:
"I am a human being, not a ghost; I recall my past lives and the merit I have bestowed. I desire to see those who bestow gifts.
When his mother heard these words, she leaped for joy without fear and consented to assist him, allowing him to give as he pleased."
My family and kin were many; my mother commanded that I be provided with offerings.
I was respected and loved by all, and none who saw me failed to rejoice.
At the very moment of my birth, that household flourished and prospered.
Because of these śramaṇas, I was named Śrīra.
Thereupon I practiced giving, providing for all who were poor and lowly.
Having encountered a Samyaksaṃbuddha, I then left home to follow the Way.
At birth his family flourished and prospered; upon falling to the ground he was able to speak.
For this reason he was named Śrī, and his name spread naturally.
At birth his family had nothing to covet, nor did they have any cause for fear.
Out of faith, he left the household life to study, becoming fully endowed with all supernormal powers.
He was held in high esteem by the sovereign, and by the ministers and the common people;
he received abundant offerings of food, clothing, bedding, and all necessities for his comfort.
Thus Śrīlā, amidst the community of bhikṣus at Lake Anavatapta,
spoke of her own past deeds: "In the past,
I used to sell medicine in the kingdom of Bandhumatī."
During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he venerated the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, there were those who were ill and emaciated;
he administered medicines to treat their ailments and provided various medicinal herbs for the sense organs to bestow upon the bhikṣus.
For one year, he provided for all the monks so that they lacked for nothing;
